OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $\epsilon>0$. Is there some set $A\subset \mathbb{N}$ of density $>1-\epsilon$ such that $a_1\cdots a_r=b_1\cdots b_s$ with $a_i,b_j\in A$ can only hold when $r=s$?
Similarly, can one always find a set $A\subset\{1,\ldots,N\}$ with this property of size $\geq (1-o(1))N$?
#786: [Er65][Er69,p.81][Er73,p.132][Er80,p.114]
number theory
An example of such a set with density $1/4$ is given by the integers $\equiv 2\pmod{4}$.
Selfridge constructed such a set with density $1/e-\epsilon$ for any $\epsilon>0$: let $p_1<\cdots<p_k$ be a sequence of large consecutive primes such that\[\sum_{i=1}^k\frac{1}{p_i}<1<\sum_{i=1}^{k+1}\frac{1}{p_i},\]and let $A$ be those integers divisible by exactly one of $p_1,\ldots,p_k$.
For the second question the set of integers with a prime factor $>N^{1/2}$ give an example of a set with size $\geq (\log 2)N$. Erdős could improve this constant slightly. Such an improvement is given by Tao in the comments, taking $A$ to be the set of all integers with exactly one prime factor $>N^{\frac{1}{1+\sqrt{e}}}$, which has size $\approx 0.8285 N$.
In [Er65] Erdős reports that Ruzsa proved the maximal size of such an $A$ is $\leq (1-c)N$ for some constant $c>0$ for large $N$, but the proof 'is not yet published'. It is presumably the following.
For any such $A$ we can define an associated additive function $f$ by letting $f(a_1\cdots a_r)=r$, and then $A=\{ n: f(n)=1\}$. A result of Erdős, Ruzsa, and Sárkzözy [ERS73] then implies that there exists a constant $c>0$ such that, for all sufficiently large $N$, $\lvert A\rvert\leq (1-c)N$. In [ERS73] they indicate that their method should be able to obtain this with $c=1/10$. In the comments Tao explains how a result of Granville and Soundararajan [GrSo01] implies\[\lvert A\rvert\leq (1-c+o(1))N\]for an explicit constant $c\approx 0.1715$, and this is the best possible (see also [121]).
Theorem 2 from [ERS73] also implies a negative answer to the first question, in that the density is at most $1/2$.
The above all assumes that repetition is allowed amongst the $a_i$ and $b_i$ in this condition. It is ambiguous in the original sources cited whether this was intended or not. If we insist the products are of distinct elements then this is a weaker condition on $A$, and the above questions are still open.
The formulation in [Er80] is clear that repetitions are not allowed, but also claims that Ruzsa had shown the answer to both questions is no in this case (and that Ruzsa had shown that the upper density of $A$ is $<1/e$ if $A$ is infinite with this property); it is possible that Erdős was mistakenly thinking of the above results, in which repetitions are allowed.
See also [421] and [795].
Additional thanks to: Rishika Agrawal, ebarschkis, and Terence Tao

 As long as one is in the regime where $r,s$ is much smaller than $N$ then there should not be much distinction as far as probabilistic arguments are concerned between sampling with repetition and sampling without repetition (they will be contiguous distributions). Sampling with repetition tends to be slightly easier to work with at a technical level, so I phrased the sketch of an argument there, but I do not foresee much difficulty in modifying it to sampling without repetition. But the current wording is ambiguous with regards to which variant is intended.
EDIT: I looked at the references for the problem (the [Er65] is p.182 by the way). None of the three references make it clear (they refer to products such as $\prod_{r=1}^{l_1} a_{i_r}$ without saying exactly what the $i_r$ are), but in nearby problems they talk about products of distinct elements, so I would be inclined to agree with the formal interpretation that each products is intended to consist of distinct elements. (Otherwise one could probably get some collision using a huge number of copies of each element on linear algebraic grounds.)

 Agreed on contiguity for $r,s\ll N$. Just noting that my linear-algebra reduction idea would use powers $a^m$ as repeated factors, so it would apply to the multiset variant but not directly to the no-repetition variant.
EDIT: That is pretty much what my reduction idea basically does in the repetitions-allowed variant: any integer relation $\sum_i m_i v(a_i)=0$ yields $\prod_i a_i^{m_i^+}=\prod_i a_i^{m_i^-}$, and interpreting $a^m$ as $m$ repeats gives a collision with $r\neq s$ unless $\sum_i m_i=0$.
Hence repetitions-allowed forces $A\subset{n:F(n)=1}$ for a totally additive $F$, and ERS then gives density $\le 1/2$ (and $|A\cap[1,N]|\le (1-c)N)$. So if the intended problem is open, I would think that strongly suggests the distinct-elements interpretation.

 For the repetitions version of the second problem, the above arguments combined with the result of Granville and Soundarajan in my comment from 18 October 2025 implies that one can in fact take c to be the Hall-Montgomery constant 0.1715..., which is sharp by the example given there; one simply converts the additive function $f(n)$ in the commentary to the multiplicative function $(-1)^{f(n)}$, with $A$ now contained in the level set $\{ n \leq N: (-1)^{f(n)}= -1\}$.
I would tentatively conjecture the same bound also holds for the no-repetitions problem; this is actually quite similar to a conjecture I made in my paper on #121, also linked to in the October comment.

 I don't know of any better bound in either direction. The set $\{(-1)^{f(n)}=-1\}$ can have density at most $1/2$ by Wirsing's theorem (in fact the density can be computed exactly in terms of an Euler product) and this is sharp by considering the Liouville function (corresponding to $f = \omega$), but this set is only an upper bound for $\{ f(n) = 1\}$ and not a lower bound.

 If one takes $A$ to be the set of $n$ with exactly one prime factor greater than $N^{1/(1+\sqrt{e})}$, one gets a set of density $1-c+o(1)$ where 
$$c = 1 - \log(1+\sqrt{e}) + 2 \int_1^{\sqrt{e}} \frac{\log t}{t+1}\ dt = 0.171500\dots$$
is the Hall-Montgomery constant; this is presumably what the "slight improvement of the constant $\log 2=1-0.3086\dots$" by Erdos optimizes to (see Theorem 9 of this recent paper of Fleiner et al. for a closely related calculation; Erdos's own calculation likely closely follows that in page 585 of this paper of Erdos, Sarkozy, and Sos). $A$ can also be defined as the set $\{ n \leq N: f(n)=-1\}$, where $f$ is the completely multiplicative function with $f(p)=-1$ if $p > N^{1/(1+\sqrt{e})}$ and $f(p)=+1$ otherwise. Corollary 1 of this paper of Granville and Soundararajan shows that this is the best density one can get from such a completely multiplicative construction, and one can tentatively conjecture that this is in fact the optimal density for the second part of this problem. (A similar line of reasoning would lead to a predicted upper bound of 1/2 for the density in the first part of the problem, but I doubt that this would be sharp, as I do not think that constructions arising from completely multiplicative functions are the most important case here.)
A recent paper of mine has a similar conjecture relating to #121. In the spirit of that paper, one might try to recover Ruzsa's result (i.e., answer the second part of this problem in the negative) by constructing some reasonably uniform probability measure on $\{1,\dots,N\}$ with the property that the probability of a collision $a_1 \dots a_r = b_1 \dots b_s$ for some suitable distinct $r,s$ is non-zero (with $a_1,\dots,a_r,b_1,\dots,b_s$ drawn independently using this probability measure), and also does not change much if one fixes any one of the $a_1,\dots,a_r,b_1,\dots,b_s$, so that one still gets collisions even if one conditions to an event of probability $1-o(1)$. As long as the probability measure is contiguous with the uniform measure in the sense that events that occur with probability $1-o(1)$ in one measure, also occur with probability $1-o(1)$ in the other, this should recover Ruzsa's result. 
Based on the above literature, it may also be worth considering as model problems variants of the problem in which density is not measure with respect to the uniform measure on $\{1,\dots,N\}$, but instead with the logarithmic measure (with each $1 \leq n \leq N$ having a density proportional to $1/n$), or a zeta distribution (with $n$ ranging over all natural numbers, but with density proportional to $1/n^s$ for some $s>1$). The limiting distribution of products such as $a_1 \dots a_r$ may be easier to analyze for such distributions, though the threshold densities will likely be different from the ones predicted above.
Neither of the two AI tools above picked up on this connection; this is a good reminder that such tools are not infallible, and should be used in conjunction with more traditional literature search methods, rather than serve as a complete replacement for them.

A partial proof 
claimed by Declan Gessel (using GPT-6 Astra (Codex)).
 Summary:
 We answer part (i) negatively for distinct factors. If A is a set of positive integers with natural density δ, and finite subsets of A with equal products always have equal cardinalities, then δ ≤ 7/8. The finite-set question (ii) is not settled.
Call a prime p good if infinitely many x have both x and px in A. Every member of A has a prime divisor that is not good; otherwise fresh pairs (x,px) give equal products with different numbers of distinct factors. Assuming density greater than 7/8, select finitely many such bad primes with reciprocal sum between 1/2 and 1. Their dilates pA overlap A only finitely. Counting their union and bounding pairwise intersections by multiples of pq yields a contradiction.
The proof is checked in Lean. The bound concerns natural density, not upper natural density.
 Notes:
 Historical qualification: Erdős (1980), p. 114, reports a stronger unpublished negative result of Ruzsa in the subset formulation. The current problem page notes possible confusion with the repetition-allowed version. This is an independently derived, machine-checked argument; no priority over Ruzsa is claimed.
